To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the SLICK locus is a 0.80 Mb region on BTA 20 that contains two candidate genes, SKP2 and SPFE2.

we have refined the SLICK locus location on BTA20, identified two candidate genes, SKP2 and SFEF2, within the region and have identified two distinct haplotype blocks within the region that are unique to slick individuals.

we identified a 0.7Mb consensus region on BTA20 containing SKP2 and SPFE2 as candidate genes for the SLICK coat locus, that we identified three unique haplotypes in the SLICK locus that were not present in non-slick breeds, and that the SLICK locus in Senepol and Carora may be different than the SLICK locus of Romosinuano.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the SLICK locus and its potential candidate genes, as well as the identification of genetic similarities and differences among the three slick breeds.
the genetic characterization of a unique coat trait, the slick coat, in tropically adapted breeds of cattle.
identifying genetic markers and haplotypes associated with the SLICK locus in three tropically adapted cattle populations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a single SLICK locus on chromosome 20, but there are two distinct mutations that affect the slick coat phenotype in Senepol, Romosinuano, and Carora.
the SLICK locus is a complex locus that is not fixed in all slick cattle.
the SLICK trait in the three slick breeds is likely due to two mutations in SKP2 and/or SPEF2.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the SLICK locus is a complex trait with multiple mutations that may have arisen independently in different populations.

the SLICK locus is likely the result of a single mutation that occurred in a common ancestor to Senepol, Romosinuano, and Carora, with a second mutation in Carora that is not present in Senepol and/or Romosinuano.
SLICK locus is located on BTA20 and contains two haplotype patterns with zero frequency in ancestral non-slick breeds.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the SLICK phenotype is a result of two independent mutations in the same region of BTA20, which occurred in two different populations of cattle.
the SLICK locus is highly conserved across the three slick breeds and that SLICK is likely an ancestral trait that is maintained through selection.
the SLICK locus is located in a 0.7 Mb region containing SKP2 and SPPF2, and that the slick phenotype in the Carora breed is distinct from that of the other breeds.
